extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, theology, canon law, and Hobbes' Leviathan
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains Hobbes' criteria for when scriptures, councils, and ecclesiastical officers acquire legal/authoritative force under civil sovereignty, and the rules for election and maintenance of church officers. Focuses on canonical status, ordination, offices, and clerical revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripture becomes Law only by civil sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: The Scriptures of the Old and New Testament were never made Laws, but by the Soveraign Civill Power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues repeatedly that a Law is the command of the sovereign to whom we have given authority; therefore writings (e.g., the New Testament) are only obligatory Canons — i.e., laws — where the lawful civil power has made them so. Absent such sovereign enactment, Scripture supplies counsel and doctrine but not binding civil law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between the two Tables of the Decalogue
rubrics_metrics.description: The first Table containeth the law of Soveraignty ... The second Table containeth the Duty of one man towards another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes distinguishes the first table (prohibitions related to worship and obedience to sovereign authority: 'Non habebis Deos alienos coram me', no images, not take God's name in vain, observe the Sabbath) from the second table (natural-law duties between persons: honor parents, not kill, not commit adultery, not steal, not corrupt judgment, not even design injury in the heart). He treats second-table precepts as Laws of Nature, universal and binding beyond Israel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moses (and High Priest) as civil sovereign canonizing Mosaic law
rubrics_metrics.description: Moses, and Aaron, and the succeeding High Priests were the Civill Soveraigns. Therefore hitherto, the Canonizing, or making of the Scripture Law, belonged to the Civill Soveraigne.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Israelites 'obliged themselves ... to obey Moses' (Exod. 20.19), Moses's propounded laws became civil law. Hobbes uses this historical claim to illustrate that the act of making Scripture binding was done by those who held civil sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public promulgation and custody confer canonical status
rubrics_metrics.description: This Law ... was written by Moses himself in a Book; and delivered into the hands of the 'Priests, and to the Elders of Israel' ... 'to be put in the side of the Arke'; the King was to keep a copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes treats the writing, public display (on stones), custody by priests/elders, and keeping of copies by kings (Deut. 17.18) as elements in making a law public and canonical; recovery and public acceptance (as in Josiah's discovery) are also required for a text to function as the Law of the commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts of councils are counsel, not laws unless backed by sovereign authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeing then the Acts of Councell of the Apostles, were then no Laws, but Councells; much lesse are Laws the Acts of any other Doctors, or Councells since, if assembled without the Authority of the Civill Soveraign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although councils may 'lay a burthen' on those who have embraced the doctrine (Acts 15.28), Hobbes insists their decrees are not civil laws binding on all unless the civil sovereign authorizes them; councils' acts are binding as teaching or as obligations of those within the ecclesiastical body, not as enforceable civil commands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostolic commission is persuasive, not legislative
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Saviour Christs Commission to his Apostles ... was to Proclaim his Kingdome ... and to Teach all Nations ... but not to call for fire from heaven to destroy them, nor to compell them to obedience by the Sword. In all which there is nothing of Power, but of Perswasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes emphasizes that apostles were sent as teachers ('Sheep unto Wolves'), not as sovereigns; thus their writings and acts are persuasive religious instruction, not civil laws, unless later adopted by sovereign authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical status requires sovereign or lawful assembly's acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Scripture of the New Testament is there only Law, where the lawfull Civill Power hath made it so. And there also the King, or Soveraign, maketh it a Law to himself; by which he subjecteth himselfe ... to God himselfe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where a ruler personally adopts religious texts as law (subjecting himself), binding civil force originates from sovereign enactment. Hobbes notes that private acceptance by converts is not equivalent to public legal obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for Apostleship: witness of the Resurrection or prior company with Christ
rubrics_metrics.description: This Testimony, was the specificall, and essentiall mark; whereby the Apostleship was distinguished ... as being necessary for an Apostle, either to have seen our Saviour after his Resurrection, or to have conversed with him before, and seen his works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes cites Acts (e.g., Matthias, Paul's Damascus vision) to argue that being a competent apostle required being a witness to Christ's resurrection (or having conversed with him before the Passion). This is presented as an essential qualification that distinguished apostles from other ecclesiastical ministers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election and ordination by the congregation/assembly (plurality of suffrages)
rubrics_metrics.description: They ordained Elders by the Holding up of Hands in every Congregation ... to ordain an Officer in any of the Cities, was no more but to bring the people together, to elect them by plurality of Votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes reads the Greek cheirotonesantes as evidence that elders/bishops were chosen by the congregation's votes (holding up hands, balls, beans, stones). The apostles acted as presidents to call assemblies, pronounce results, and give benediction (consecration), but the choice belonged to the people assembled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bishops/presbyters were local elections, not appointments by predecessors
rubrics_metrics.description: We find not, that ever any Bishop of Rome appointed his successor. For they were a long time chosen by the People ... though they afterwards were chosen, first, by the whole Clergy ..., yet never any was appointed to the succession by his predecessor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues against the notion that ecclesiastical offices passed by appointment from predecessors; historically the people (and later clergy/cardinals) elected bishops, supporting his broader claim that coercive appointment required civil sovereign regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magisterial vs ministerial offices and their functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Of Ecclesiastical Officers in the time of the Apostles, some were Magisteriall, some Ministeriall. Magisteriall were the Offices of preaching ... and of teaching the Rules of Faith and Manners ... Ministeriall was the Office of Deacons ... appointed to the administration of the secular necessities of the Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes distinguishes offices that teach and administer sacraments (magisterial: apostles, bishops, elders, pastors, doctors) from those that manage secular tasks (ministerial: deacons). This distinction matters for who may perform spiritual acts (e.g., conferring the Holy Ghost) and who serves the congregation's temporal needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection qualities for deacons/ministries: honest report, full of Holy Ghost and wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Brethren looke you out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost, and of Wisdome, whom we may appoint over this businesse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes quotes Acts 6 as the standard for choosing deacons: the congregation should select men of good reputation, filled with the Holy Ghost, and wise. This gives specific moral/spiritual criteria for appointment to ministerial roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may confer the Holy Ghost and confirm baptism
rubrics_metrics.description: It was necessary for the conferring of the Holy Ghost, that their Baptisme should be administred, or confirmed by a Minister of the Word, not by a Minister of the Church. To confirm the Baptisme of those that Philip the Deacon had Baptized, the Apostles ... Peter, and John ... conferred on them ... those graces that were signs of the Holy Spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes notes a procedural distinction: deacons could baptize, but only 'ministers of the word' (apostles/bishops) could confirm and confer the Holy Ghost. This establishes a functional boundary on sacramental authority between ministerial and magisterial offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical maintenance and revenues derive from civil/public authority
rubrics_metrics.description: To the Tribe of Levi were assigned certain Cities ... for their portion, they were to have the tenth of the fruits of the land of their Brethren ... For God being then King ... it is manifest, that the Right of Tythes, and Offerings was constituted by the Civill Power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes explains that clerical livelihood (tithes, oblations, priestly portions) was public revenue assigned under the civil power (God as King or later human kings). Thus the right to tithes and other ecclesiastical revenues depends on the public/commonwealth's authority and disposition.
